The Rooks were held to a goalless draw at The Dripping Pan last Saturday by a stubborn Stanway Rovers side who started the day bottom of the Isthmian Premier Division table.

However, they responded well in midweek by avoiding a Sussex Senior Cup upset at 21st-placed Isthmian South East Division side Eastbourne Town, winning 2-1 at The Saffrons.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

After both games, manager Craig Nelson admitted there were areas for his side to improve.

Following the Stanway game, which was Nelson’s 100th match in charge of the Rooks, the 40-year-old noted: “For me, we had too many players [who] it felt like [were] going through the motions.

“The intensity felt a bit low, and the ball speed was low. We breached their backline so many times, but the quality beyond that, for me, was a little bit too low to come away with a victory.

“Other than the first chance in the early minutes from Noel [Fisher], where for me he should score, I don't remember us having a clear-cut chance. So, not a great day at the office, in my opinion.”.

Despite being more fluent in attack at Eastbourne Town, with an impressive performance from debutant Kwesi Ntim playing a big part, Lewes still lacked some ruthlessness after going 2-0 up.

Recent findings suggest that afterwards, Nelson mentioned: “I think we had moments. They're always going to make the game difficult for us, and the conditions obviously don't help.

“We had some good moments in the second half. Probably more opportunities to score. On another day, you probably leave here with a bit more.

It has been revealed that “I think sometimes in cup games, the performance is secondary to actually progressing. We wanted to make sure that we put a strong outfit out because we want to progress in the cup, and we've done that, so happy days.”.

Lewes can celebrate a first appearance in the Senior Cup’s Quarter-Finals since the 2019-20 season as a result, and will learn their opponents when the draw is expected to take place in the next fortnight.

In the meantime, the Rooks make the 171-mile round trip to Ramsgate FC this Saturday, with the Rams sitting just three points behind Nelson’s side in 6th place.

The Kent side are the third-highest goalscorers in the league so far with 38 goals from 17 games, while Callum Jones’ 10 league strikes make him the division’s second-best individual goalscorer.

It has been revealed that nelson mentioned: “Ramsgate is a really hostile place to go. They're going to be quick and physical, so we have to make sure that we bring that work ethic and match exactly what the game demands of us.”.

Liverpool Confidential: Latest on new deals for Virgil van Dijk and Alisson as European giants circle, how Reds are trying to turbocharge academy recruitment and Joshua Abe's comeback

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:01 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 18 November 2026.
  • European clubs are on red alert over the futures of Liverpool stars Virgil van Dijk and Alisson – despite both players being keen to extend their contracts at Anfield.
  • It has been revealed that one source told me this week that AC Milan and other Italian clubs have been sniffing around Van Dijk for some time, with talks ongoing internally at those sides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:01 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 18 November 2026.

European clubs are on red alert over the futures of Liverpool stars Virgil van Dijk and Alisson – despite both players being keen to extend their contracts at Anfield.

It has been revealed that one source told me this week that AC Milan and other Italian clubs have been sniffing around Van Dijk for some time, with talks ongoing internally at those sides. Milan owner Gerry Cardinale and influential adviser Zlatan Ibrahimovic are stated to be huge admirers of Van Dijk, who turns 36 next summer.

Italy was also a potential destination for Alisson last summer after Juventus held talks with his camp. At one point, Juve fancied their chances of signing him.

Both players will, as it stands, be able to negotiate a free transfer to overseas clubs from January 1, but both Alisson, 34, and Van Dijk, 35, want to stay at Anfield.

It puts the ball in the court of Julian Ward, Liverpool's sporting director, who must decide what to do next.

There had been a long-standing unwritten rule at owners Fenway Sports Group of never extending deals for those over the age of 30, but this was broken in the exceptional cases of Van Dijk and Mohamed Salah 18 months ago, after the pair led Liverpool to their 20th league title.

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is keen to stay at the club despite reported interest from his native Brazil.

Reds captain Virgil van Dijk (right) also wants to extend his contract at Liverpool – even though AC Milan are showing interest.

Despite both players wanting to stay on Merseyside, there is understandably a great deal of interest from around the world in taking them on, with local reports linking several Brazilian clubs to Alisson recently.

Van Dijk is a regular at Liverpool youth-team matches, which indicates his love of the club but may also lead to suggestions the Dutchman will move into youth coaching when he does hang up his boots. He took the first-team squad to the Liverpool FC Museum recently to learn more about the club's history – further highlighting his passion for the Reds.

Interest from abroad only strengthens the hands of Alisson and Van Dijk, however, when it comes to their demands over the salary and duration of their new deals.

Alexis Mac Allister is another with an uncertain future, though his father and agent Carlos is hoping to hold talks with Liverpool in the coming weeks. The Argentine's future is less of a pressing concern for the Reds, though, given his deal runs until summer 2028.

Joe Gomez and Kostas Tsimikas are among the other players whose contracts are up in June next year.

It has been revealed that it was around this time last year that the wheels started to fall off the Arne Slot machine. The Dutchman was eventually sacked and we have not heard much from him since. One question I am often asked is what is Slot up to – and why has he fallen off the face of the earth?

Well, I can reveal the former Reds boss is biding his time and enjoying holidays with loved ones, including several trips to Ibiza. Slot and his son Joep have also visited South America, taking in games in Argentina and Brazil.

Slot, who has also been attending matches at home, turned down the Netherlands national team job and a lucrative gig in Saudi Arabia. He also rejected approaches in the summer from clubs including AC Milan, who eventually plumped for former Manchester United boss Ruben Amorim.

He is waiting for the right opportunity and does not believe his stock has fallen in the same way, for example, as several axed United or Chelsea bosses. After all, Slot won the Premier League title and would be a fine hire for most clubs around Europe.

Former Liverpool boss Arne Slot (centre, bottom row) watches the Dutch Eredivisie match between Heerenveen and his old club Feyenoord earlier this month.

Slot is waiting for the right job to come up – emboldened by the knowledge he is a Premier League winner.

…but AI report makes grim reading for Arne.

A couple of interesting bits to pick out from the fantastic Global State of Football report by PLAIER, a firm spearheading the use of artificial intelligence in football.

Liverpool finished bottom of the table last season in PLAIER’s ranking of every team's coaches based on resources and how they performed – Regis Le Bris at Sunderland was top.

Industry observers note that the Reds were in the bottom three for coaching efficiency, suggesting that squad quality alone is no guarantee of success. For a more in-depth look at the report, click here.

Reds hunt for academy recruitment guru.

Liverpool are in the process of hiring an academy ‘talent ID lead’ to help with their youth recruitment.

It has been revealed that regular readers of this column will know this area is a key metric Anfield chiefs measure success by. They are now hiring someone responsible for leading the identification and recruitment of academy talent between the ages of 13 and 18 across the UK and Ireland.

Notable recent arrivals from other academies at this age include current first-teamers Rio Ngumoha, Conor Bradley, Trey Nyoni and James McConnell.

Kop Kids: Amazing Abe lights up England duty.

Confidential readers will recall I revealed on October 15 that Joshua Abe was ahead of schedule in his recovery from a shoulder injury and set for just another month on the sidelines. And Abe was indeed on the pitch representing England Under 17s exactly a month later, scoring against Montenegro and then again against Poland on Saturday.

According to recent reports, in the last 12 months, the 16-year-old has 14 goals and four assists in just over 1,200 minutes played. Those are phenomenal numbers and it would not be a surprise to see the winger back in the first-team training group again soon.

Joshua Abe has recovered from a shoulder injury and was back in action for England Under 17s this week.

Fancy running the line, Andoni?

In a recent development, in the last break, the boss was spotted at the women’s Merseyside Derby. Now, he has been pictured at a local Sunday League match, taking pictures with youngsters who could not believe their luck.

These may seem like small gestures but they are a helpful way of winning hearts and minds among a fanbase whose pleas for Slot to take an active interest in all aspects of the club sometimes fell on deaf ears.

Manchester United are in town on Sunday, in case you needed reminding.

Since winning the Premier League title last year, Liverpool’s league record against the 'Major Six' is played 12, won two, drawn three, lost seven. That must improve, starting on Sunday, and there can be no excuses around a newly introduced-manager bounce for Mauricio Pochettino - who will barely have had time to find his parking space at Carrington by the time he comes to Anfield.

It has been revealed that liverpool need to see more from their significant-money signings Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, who have been excellent for most of the season but poor in some high-profile fixtures, such as the home defeats by Manchester City and Arsenal. Across his 19 games against Liverpool, Pochettino has only won three matches, drawing five and losing 11.

On the Late Football Club show, Olivier Tallaron revealed that four key players were going to extend: Ousmane Dembele, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Desire Doue and Matvey Safonov.

The Ballon d’Or winner has agreed with the two-time European cham.

pions on salary and on the length of his newly introduced deal, which will run until June 2030. As for the other three named, their contracts will be extended until June 2032. Everything is said to be almost wrapped up, as the extensions are due to be unveiled in the coming days, according to the same source.

It has been revealed that at the same time, the Parisian club have opened negotiations with five other key players in the squad: Marquinhos, Warren Zaire-Emery, Vitinha, Achraf Hakimi and Nuno Mendes. PSG are offering their captain a one-year extension, which could take his deal until June 2029.

Paris are aiming for long-term signings until June 2032 with the four others named, who are younger and represent the future of the club.

Sources indicate that overall, the Brazilian defender, the Paris academy product, the Moroccan full-back and the two Portugal internationals would also be rather willing to continue their adventure in Paris. It remains to be seen whether the negotiations will again be fruitful.

It is, in any case, good news for PSG, who had already extended Willian Pacho and Joao Neves last year. The Parisian club intend, and are well placed, to keep the core of their two-time reigning European champions for the long term.

It should also be noted that the French side want to extend two academy products: Quentin Ndjantou and David Boly.

Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

Sources indicate that it will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Sources indicate that russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”.

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

In a recent development, at the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”.

Recent findings suggest that this was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

According to recent reports, “It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”.

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”.

Industry observers note that no. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9.

Tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw.

According to recent reports, “Very difficult to understand. We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is the different to all the (other) tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”.

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:.

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”.

Lewis Hamilton notes this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

Sources indicate that “The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”.

“I love this energy [from the crowd]. Significant, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

Recent findings suggest that “I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”.

A reminder that Isack Hadjar will drop from third to eighth after his grid penalty.

Recent findings suggest that “It is fantastic. We have been trying many grand prix to get pole. Sometimes a bit closer than others but to finally get it, from where we started the season, pretty incredible. I am happy with today and, for sure, I am going to try and win tomorrow. When you start first, that is the target.”.

Massive disappointment that for Russell. After his win in Baku, where he said he finally felt hooked up to the car, he was desperate to build the momentum. P8, four places behind Antonelli, was not what he would have had in mind. Has it all to do in the race tomorrow.

According to recent reports, excellent (though not unexpected) pole for Verstappen, and a very good P2 for Hamilton. Could be some fireworks on the front row tomorrow.

*Hadjar’s three-place grid penalty will drop him down to eighth place for the race tomorrow.

Neither of the Red Bulls can improve in the first sector but it is those behind them who need significant improvements. The two Ferraris are going along nicely at the start of their final flying laps. Hadjar is unable to improve despite a purple final sector. Verstappen then goes fastest in the final sector and improves his advantage at the top.

That means that Verstappen takes pole in Malaysia, which is the first time this season that Red Bull have taken pole position. It has been revealed that the championship leader sets a decent middle sector where he loses no more time to Verstappen. As it stands he would put himself third before the others do their final runs. He comes across the line in P3 but will have the likes of Hamilton, Piastri, Leclerc, Norris and Russell trying to surpass him.

Russell is the first across the line and sets a time of a 1:36.032. He does not last long at the top as he is immediately displaced by Hadjar, who is half a second quicker.

Hamilton then comes over the line in second, just ahead of his teammate Leclerc. Piastri puts himself between the two Ferraris.

What about Verstappen? The man who won here the last time we were in Malaysia continues his great form today and goes quickest by more than three tenths.

Industry observers note that russell is the first man to head out for his first flying lap in Q3. Antonelli has remained in the pits with just one fresh set of softs remaining. Verstappen, who right now feels like the favourite for pole, will be one of the last across the line in these first attempts of Q3.

The fight for pole position in Sepang begins now as the green light is on at the end of the pit lane to get Q3 going.

Antonelli, due to that lap time deletion in Q2, has just one new set of softs for Q3, which could prove costly in his attempts to try and take pole.

As the young Italian starts his flying lap, there is no-one else out on track so no traffic. He is a lot more cautious at turn six this time than last time, when he had his lap time deleted.

This is now a lot of pressure on the championship leader; any mistake now and he will not make Q3. His teammate Russell is only in seventh.

Antonelli was fourth fastest but has had his lap time deleted for exceeding track limits at turn six. That is a massive moment in Q2 and could prove problematic if he gets into Q3. Antonelli appeared to be confused when he was told about his lap deletion over team radio but the on-board view looked pretty clear-cut.

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

Sources indicate that it’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

Industry observers note that “Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

According to recent reports, he added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”.

According to recent reports, the two Ferraris are on medium tyres but Leclerc still puts himself into second place. He is then displaced by Hamilton, who slots in behind Verstappen. Good times from the Ferraris on the mediums.

This will be one of if not the hottest qualifying sessions of the season, so much so that we are seeing umbrellas going up to get some shade from the sun rather than sheltering from any rain.

We know Lindblad will be at the back and is very likely to be joined there by Colapinto, who is not going to be qualifying high up in the top ten in his Alpine.

Haas have announced that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

Aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:.

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to matter a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

Sources indicate that “Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti stated. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really key that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”.

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

It has been revealed that “The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”.

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Industry observers note that almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:.

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso).

Recent findings suggest that with Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Sources indicate that verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car patch since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

Industry observers note that this race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

Redz Live will bring live music to the club's Redz Bar, Broadfield Stadium every Friday night starting from Friday, February 5.

The project is being organised by Phil Atkinson, who has been responsible for the music programme at the renowned Half Moon Putney since 2017 where he has established a regular programme of emerging artists and live music.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

According to recent reports, phil also organises weekly live music events at Sutton United FC. He noted: “I'm delighted to bring that experience to Crawley.

“The aim is to establish Redz Live as a regular destination for live entertainment in the town, bringing some of the UK's best tribute bands and live music acts to the area.”.

Phil has already got a fantastic programme of shows confirmed, including tributes to David Bowie, Led Zeppelin, Bon Jovi, Fleetwood Mac, The Killers and Queen.

“It's an exciting opportunity to bring something newly introduced to Crawley, make further use of the stadium outside matchdays and create a regular entertainment offering for the local community. The demonstrates will bring in revenue to the club which is becoming increasingly important.”.

And it was the community feel that attracted Phil to start the venture with the football club. “I was chatting to my colleague at The Half Moon Putney about football and he mentioned that his Mum, Rhona Kaye, has been running the bars at Crawley Town FC for years,” he remarked.

Sources indicate that "We went down together to watch an evening match and I loved the atmosphere and the space is perfect for putting gigs on. It's a real community feel at the club and when I mentioned it could be a good thing to work together on some gigs. They are really enthusiastic and I'm excited to be building something special there.”.

In a recent development, and he added that football clubs are great for these kinds of gigs and that the Redz Bar is perfect for gigs. “They are often at the heart of communities with a broad range of people connected to the club. The venue itself is a perfect shape for live music and the infrastructure is all in place for busy matchdays,” said Phil. “There are great transport links back into town, a large free car park and a great bar that is used to pouring pints as promptly as possible!”.

You can find out more about the project, see the full programme and buy tickets at www.redzlive.com.

#37783. Why the moral lessons of Scottish lower league football really are vital – Craig Levein

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (994 w)

Why the moral lessons of Scottish lower league football really are vital – Craig Levein

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotsman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we often take pride in Scotland in our more authentic, less corrupted professional football.
  • In a recent development, the recent Man City scandal has only served to sharpen this contrast.
  • Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we often take pride in Scotland in our more authentic, less corrupted professional football. Sure, it lacks the glitz and glamour of the English game, awash with American and Middle Eastern money, but as a result it has remained more rooted in our communities, and more accessible to the working class fans who made the game great in the first place.

In a recent development, the recent Man City scandal has only served to sharpen this contrast. While Pep Guardiola’s teams played undeniably beautiful football, the subsequent revelations of financial impropriety have put the validity of their titles under question and damaged the sporting credibility of the Premier League.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It has shone a light on the trade-offs English football has had to make: creating an elite, globally renowned product, but at the cost of affording dubious characters free rein over long-standing, treasured community institutions.

READ MORE: Scotland's most beautiful football ground is such a pastoral delight that even Subbuteo noticed.

Scotland’s approach has been different. There is less money, to be sure, but that has insulated the Scottish game from some of this scandal. As a result, it feels more real, a purer form of the game.

However, the truth is that Scottish football is a tough place to ply your trade. This is especially true in the lower divisions, where I started my career with Cowdenbeath in the early 1980s.

Football at this level couldn’t feel further removed from the clashes between Wall Street billionaires and petrostates so common south of the border. It was hard work and often brutal. Although we might take pride in it, the undeniable truth is that for many clubs further down the pyramid, life is tough. Razor thin margins, poor facilities, and low attendances can make it demanding work both on and off the pitch.

It’s hardly surprising then, contrary to how we might see ourselves, that Scottish clubs are not immune to finding themselves reliant on financial benefactors whose interest in them, and in the areas they represent, is passing. When the money dries up, the very existence of these clubs comes under threat.

Recent findings suggest that take Gretna FC as an example. In 2008, two years after appearing in the Scottish Cup Final, and enjoying a sustained run in the top-flight for the first time in their history, the club was forced into liquidation. Gretna’s owner, Brooks Mileson, who died later that year, was posthumously declared bankrupt.

This tragic episode shows the dangers of overreliance on financiers who promise big and briefly deliver, before things come crashing down; a similar fate very nearly befell Dumbarton FC in 2024, when the club went into administration and were only saved by a takeover at the last minute. When the worst happens, there is little that loyal, matchgoing fans can do other than pick up the pieces and start again.

Industry observers note that responsible stewardship then, in the cutthroat world of the Scottish lower divisions, is worth more than silverware. One standout example of this is my friend, Kevin Mackie, chairman of Brechin City. Since 2021, Kevin has done an incredible job stabilising the fan-owned club after a turbulent few years which saw successive relegations consign them outside the SPFL for the first time in 67 years.

Things are finally looking up; last season, the Hedgemen only narrowly missed out on promotion back into League Two. As I write, they sit third in the Lowland League and are among the favourites to challenge this season.

This is encouraging progress under Kevin’s astute leadership. It shouldn’t come as a surprise given his extensive experience as a local businessman, running successful car dealerships in the Brechin area for several decades, as well as hotels and commercial properties.

Kevin also understands what Gretna and Dumbarton seemingly didn’t: that reliance on distant financiers is fraught with danger, and that the loyalty that defines the relationship between fan and club is seldom present in the corporate world.

Kevin’s car dealership closed almost overnight when his suppliers; Renault, Nissan, and Dacia, along with their banking subsidiary RCI Bank (now Mobilize Financial Services) terminated supply and financing agreements for unclear reasons. It’s a demonstration that the dangers of financial reliance we see so often in football permeate through many other industries – though there are notable differences.

Kevin has released a legal claim in search of answers and closure, but five years on a resolution remains frustratingly elusive. This is what shocks me as a football professional. As a manager, I had to face the press immediately after each game and defend my actions. A string of bad results could easily see me fired.

Recent findings suggest that in business, and in law, this sort of direct accountability can be hard to find. The wheels turn slowly and the process is often very opaque. Troublingly, this culture is now seeping into football, as the lengthy legalistic wrangling over Man City highlights. In Scotland, we may not be immune from this.

Despite these difficulties, Kevin can take inspiration from the Brechin fans who stood by their club throughout some tough years. Dedication and loyal support define football, but business can be a different beast. Although football resembles business more and more each day, with Man City showing the ugliest side of this, we shouldn’t lose sight of what makes the game beautiful, especially north of the border.

Recent findings suggest that business and the law could learn a lot from what makes football so special, and so popular worldwide. As a dedicated steward of his local team, leading them back from some tough times, Kevin represents that as well as anyone.

Craig Levein is a former Hearts player, Scotland international and manager.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So, Crawley Town have made two substantial announcements: first, that Kevin Blackwell will be staying on as interim manager until the end of the season, and second, that the owners have released an open letter addressing fans’ concerns about the club. Here are my thoughts on both.

Kevin Blackwell staying on is the right call.

Blackwell staying at the club until the end of the season doesn’t really surprise me, as there have been plenty of signs that he would be staying a lot longer than just a couple of games.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

From the lack of news about a new manager, to the short-term deals the club has made for players like Connor Wickham and Ayman Benarous, those aren't the kind of signings you make for a manager who is about to leave.

Sources indicate that also, keeping him until the end of the season makes sense. It gives the club the stability we desperately need while also buying us time to find the right long-term permanent manager, and we have looked a lot better since he came into the club, so this feels like a good move to me.

The Owners’ Open Letter: A step in the right direction.

The other major development was that the owners have released an open letter on the club website. This was much needed, as there has been silence from the club and the owners since the departures of manager Colin Kazim-Richards and director of football Erdem Konyar last month, and this has understandably frustrated a lot of fans.

In a recent development, in the letter, they do acknowledge that mistakes have been made, and for me, that’s a good start. They are saying the right things and it shows that the owners are listening to supporters’ concerns. But actions speak louder than words, and after so many poor decisions as of late, it will take a lot more than a letter to rebuild trust, with only time will tell whether these words are hollow or not.

According to recent reports, overall, I see both announcements as a step in the right direction, as they give more clarity over the team's management and more openness from the owners. Hopefully, this is a turning point, though the results and decisions that follow will show whether it truly is, and hopefully that starts on Saturday against Fleetwood.

Tech Report: Mario Frick savours Aberdeen ‘paradise’ as heavy metal football takes precedence over cynical rave murmurings

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although he rates it as one of his best football memories, Mario Frick learned a painful lesson after scoring against Scotland at Hampden 16 years ago.
  • According to recent reports, he injured himself in the resulting melee with his Liechtenstein teammates and had to be substituted.
  • Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although he rates it as one of his best football memories, Mario Frick learned a painful lesson after scoring against Scotland at Hampden 16 years ago.

According to recent reports, he injured himself in the resulting melee with his Liechtenstein teammates and had to be substituted. “They gave me an injection but it didn't help,” he recalled. "In the seventh minute of stoppage time we lost 2-1 - which is football. It was my last year in international football, maybe my last goal for the international team at around 36-years-old.”.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

According to recent reports, it was a reminder of the perils of over celebrating. The cynic might say the new Aberdeen manager has come to the right place. The Pittodrie side haven’t scored for three matches and have recorded the fewest shots on target in the league this season.

There doesn’t seem much danger of him erupting with joy and bumping his head on the roof of those tight Pittodrie dugouts. Albeit, he will have to wait for the chance to take a bow at the stadium having replaced the sacked Stephen Robinson during the international window. Trips to Rugby Park and then Ibrox await before he can enjoy the comforts of home for the first time against Dundee at the end of this month.

According to recent reports, although there was no game on at Pittodrie on Thursday, Frick's face adorned the jumbo screen in the corner as he was officially welcomed to the club ahead of being “formally unveiled”, as the club described it. Even the empty stadium, he said, gives him “goosebumps”. He regards it as a temple. Nowhere is the reverential air more intoxicating than in the Sir Alex Ferguson Lounge, where Frick was presented to reporters for the first time. “Pure football,” he said, while gazing at the photographs adorning the walls.

In a recent development, the Aberdeen training facility at Cormack Park is better than anything he encountered in Switzerland, where he played and managed. “It is paradise,” he said. He’s clearly keen to linger awhile, to which the reply might be: Good luck with that. While he occupies a unique position as the first Liechtenstein player to become a professional footballer, Frick is slightly less exceptional when it comes to Aberdeen.

The 52-year-old is the 27th permanent manager at Pittodrie, stretching back to 1903. That averages out at about one every four-and-a-half years, which isn’t too bad. However, as many as 16 have come and gone since Ferguson left for Old Trafford 40 years ago this month. The recent anniversary celebrations – Manchester United being the ones celebrating rather than Aberdeen, who have rued the day almost ever since – were a reminder of the significance of that November’s morning in 1986, when it was announced he was heading south.

No club is immune to the difficulties of trying to replace a successful manager, as Manchester United have spent the last 13 years proving. Aberdeen have not been completely feckless without Fergie. A Scottish Cup here, a League Cup there. They haven’t been relegated either. Not yet at least.

Steering the side away from danger is Frick’s first task, starting this weekend against the only team currently below them: Kilmarnock. He knows what’s involved having taken over at his previous club, Luzern, five years ago when they were deep in relegation trouble. They parted company this summer.

“They were bottom of the table with 18 matches and 11 points when I took over there and the whole environment was similar to now,” he said. “We saved them and progressed from there. I am sure I can do the same now at Aberdeen. I am very ambitious and now it is important to get out of this situation and we want to go to the top six.”.

Sources indicate that the noises coming out of Pittodrie in recent days is that Frick likes to play ‘front foot, attacking football’, which seems to mirror the promises made by every latest manager these days. Isn’t that what Sebastien Pocognoli trumpeted when he was unveiled as Scotland manager three months ago? The alarm bells might be growing louder for Aberdeen fans. Frick explained his “heavy metal football” philosophy. “It is high pressing, it is counter pressing, it is vertical play and creating many goalscoring chances,” he said. “That is heavy metal.”.

Sources indicate that supporters will argue that anything’s better than what a team coached by Frick’s predecessor was producing. Aberdeen chief executive Adrian Bevington referred to the new manager's “warm personality” and suggested local journalists should look forward to getting to know the new man. Frick is an urbane character though one it might be advisable to avoid crossing. Trim and sporting a military haircut, he doesn’t look as if he will accept having his authority challenged.

As for the vexed question of the captaincy, with Kevin Nisbet giving the impression that the responsibility weighs heavily on him, Frick confirmed the striker will retain the armband against Kilmarnock. “Afterwards, I will have to decide what we do,” he remarked.

Frick speaks five languages with various levels of proficiency. His German and Italian are perfect. “English I need to improve,” he said. “I started learning English in school but never used it.” He recently started English tuition online “with an Australian who lives in France” with a view to working at a British club. “My only ambition now is to bring success to Aberdeen,” he said.

The fans will hope that such a zeal for self-improvement is catching. When Ferguson once ordered his players to have no fears about going to Glasgow and winning, now a sense of trepidation infects so much at the club. By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 10:00.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has revealed that Bukayo Saka will spend another four weeks on the sidelines with the quadriceps injury he sustained against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.

Saka's injury occurred in the first half of Arsenal's 2-2 draw with the Bundesliga champions on October 21, and Arteta immediately conceded at full time that the winger's problem looked severe.

Reports emerging soon after stated that Saka would miss between six and eight weeks, although Arsenal have been loath to put an exact timeframe on the Englishman's recovery just yet.

However, speaking to the media ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Newcastle United, Arteta admitted that Saka was only halfway into his recovery process and would spend the full eight weeks out.

In a recent development, "We had another test. It looks like it’s going to be an eight week injury more or less. He’s four weeks in now," the Spaniard told reporters.

Saka missing another four weeks means that the 25-year-old is set to sit out another seven matches across all competitions, including a number of heavyweight fixtures.

Arsenal host Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League next Tuesday, before ending the month with a clash of the titans against Manchester City in the Premier League.

Saka is also expected to miss matches with Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid in early December, and he will most likely be unavailable for the visit of Bournemouth on December 13 too.

However, the attacker could be fit to make his comeback against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United on December 20, until when Noni Madueke and Max Dowman will provide cover.

Dowman will serve the third of his three-game domestic suspension against Newcastle this weekend, but Madueke has earned numerous plaudits in recent weeks, having scored against Slavia Prague in the Champions League before firing the effort that led to Martin Odegaard's winner against Hull City.

Saka will likely be one of two core members of Arsenal's title-winning team to miss matches against Tottenham and Real Madrid, as Arteta also delivered negative news on Martin Zubimendi.

The midfielder appeared to hurt his hamstring in Spain's 3-2 Nations League defeat to England during the international break, and he also faces around a month on the sidelines.

Industry observers note that "He has a problem in his hamstring. The scan reveals there is an injury there he will be out for a few weeks," Arteta added on Zubimendi.

However, the 27-year-old is yet to start a Premier League game this season and was always expected to lose out to Declan Rice and Bruno Guimaraes at St James' Park tomorrow.

Arsenal are five points clear at the top of the Premier League table heading into gameweek 11 and are searching for their fourth successive win over Newcastle in the top flight.

By TOM COLLOMOSSE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Leicester have decided to end their deal with controversial sponsors BC.GAME six months ahead of schedule.

Fans expressed fury and dismay earlier this month after the club's unlicensed gambling shirt sponsor appointed an 'international porn star' as its newly introduced ambassador.

Sources indicate that now Leicester have opted to conclude the partnership – in a move welcomed by supporters. A statement on Wednesday read: ‘The decision follows constructive discussions between both parties in recent days, during which we recognised our differing commercial priorities moving forward.

‘We would like to thank BC.GAME for its support throughout its two-and-a-half-year association with Leicester City and for the constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement.

‘Supporters who have purchased a BC.GAME-branded replica shirt through official LCFC retail channels within the last 28 days (since 21 October, 2026) can return it for a full refund or exchange (subject to availability) by Wednesday 2 December.’.

Industry observers note that BC.GAME, an online casino manufacturer, had been the Foxes' primary shirt sponsor since the start of the 2024-25 season. They announced a partnership with Russian adult content creator Eva Elfie in a video on X earlier this month.

Leicester City have axed a partnership with BC.GAME, after the gambling shirt sponsor appointed 'international porn star' Eva Elfie as its upcoming ambassador.

Leicester confirmed fans who have purchased a replica shirt featuring the sponsor's name within the last 28 days can return it for a full refund or exchange by December 2.

Elfie, who has 4.8million Instagram followers, is known in Esports and gaming communities too.

In recent years, Leicester’s spectacular decline on the pitch has mirrored the relationship with their supporters.

During the years immediately before and after their stunning Premier League triumph in 2016, it was difficult to find a club more in tune with the fanbase.

But a series of baffling decisions – including the tie-up with BC.GAME – eroded trust between the club and their supporters.

Leicester are now in League One and face a long road back but sensible moves like this one suggest they are at least facing in the right direction again.

The £6million summer signing from Paderborn has become a crucial part of Celtic's midfield this season, starting 17 of the 19 matches played across all competitions thus far, and scoring four goals.

His form in Glasgow saw him break into the German national team in September, earning his first two caps under Jurgen Klopp, which was followed by his inclusion in the Germany Under-21 squad for the most recent November internationals.

However, he had to withdraw from international duty after picking up an ankle injury in a challenge with Kilmarnock’s Aaron Tshibola in the final match before the break, which Celtic won 1-0.

Celtic manager Martin O’Neill confirmed that the 22-year-old has suffered ligament damage and could be out of action until February, which would rule him out of the remainder of the Europa League campaign and the next Old Firm derby against Rangers at Ibrox on January 3.

“He’ll be out for some considerable time,” O’Neill noted as he addressed the media ahead of the Saturday’s Premiership clash with St Mirren.

“It’s a real shame, he was playing great for us. There’s talk about 10 weeks, but I spoke to Mika yesterday and he’s a quick healer.

It has been revealed that “There are things he can’t do for a while, his foot’s in a boot. He was on fire, he was doing great for us. It is a blow and it seemed so innocuous as well.

“I thought he’d been kicked, but it was the other foot he landed on and he’s just gone over on it.”.

Celtic will also assess the fitness of Benjamin Nygren ahead of the game against St Mirren with the midfielder suffering from a heel issue that saw him miss Sweden’s 1-1 draw in Poland on Tuesday.

“He didn’t train today,” O’Neill remarked. “We’ll see how he is in the morning. He’s got a sore heel. He’s been feeling it for a couple of weeks.”.

#37755. Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues

Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 157 min read (31482 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~157 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections.
  • The human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2.
  • This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment1. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. We use the model to characterize the human epithelial response to Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium at the single-cell level, uncovering the distinct gene regulatory networks that underpin luminal versus intracellular pathogen presence. Invaded epithelial cells initiate an IL-18 signalling axis that triggers cytotoxic T cell activation, resulting in epithelial shedding and barrier disruption. Overall, this work allows for the modular integration of epithelial, microbial and immune compartments, providing a versatile system for studying human intestinal physiology and pathologies.

The human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2. Controlled host–microbe interactions shape diverse aspects of human biology, including epithelial maturation and systemic immunity while maintaining a protective barrier against infection3. Conversely, dysregulated interactions contribute to pathologies such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer4.

This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5. Integration of these three components is required to meaningfully capture intestine–microbe interactions in a human-relevant setting1.

Intestinal stem cell (ISC)-derived organoids provide key inroads into human epithelial biology6. However, intestinal organoids face limitations recapitulating intestinal physiology, owing to an inaccessible lumen, culture heterogeneity, lack of biomimetic morphology and absence of non-epithelial lineages7,8. Although bioengineered 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) scaffolds have helped to overcome some of these challenges by establishing crypt–villus architecture and apical–basal access9, physiological integration of epithelial, tissue-resident immune and microbial compartments remains a major challenge1,10.

Sources indicate that here we established engineered immunocompetent human intestinal models composed of autologous tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells and small intestinal or colonic ISC-derived epithelia amenable to luminal manipulation. Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) characterization of these barriers reveal region-specific spatial niches, mucus layer formation and immune–epithelium interactions. Applying this system to Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm), we provide a single-cell multiomic view of the epithelial responses to luminal and intracellular infection. Finally, we modelled the pathogen–epithelial–immune axis, demonstrating that TRM cells respond to S.Tm invasion by cytokine release and concomitant epithelial damage, which may facilitate pathogen clearance and infection resolution.

Sources indicate that to model the human intestinal epithelium, we developed a fluidic device and microstamping technology to impart crypt-mimicking topography on an embedded ECM-like hydrogel (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Human intestinal organoids were seeded into the top reservoir of the device, where they formed a tight, polarized barrier comprising crypt units sustained by basal nutrition (Fig. 1a–d and Extended Data Fig. 1b–e).

To characterize the morphology, cellular composition and patterning of the epithelium, we developed a 3D-printed ‘histomold’ for simultaneous embedding and perpendicular sectioning of up to 50 engineered epithelia (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and mIF staining demonstrated histological and cell-type patterning similarity to donor-matched primary tissue (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Figs. 1g and 2a–c). In addition, a duodenal dual reporter line stably labelling chromatin (H2BC4–mTurquoise2) and LGR5+ stem cells (LGR5–IRES-NLS-mScarlet3) confirmed LGR5 ISC localization to the crypt bottom (Fig. 1f). By day 10, the thick epithelium contained proliferative SOX9+ and Ki67+ cells primarily confined to the crypt, whereas mature enterocytes (APOA4+ in the duodenum, and FABP6+ in the ileum) and colonocytes (CA1+) were enriched within inter-crypt regions (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 3a–f), with αDEF5+ Paneth cells detected in some small intestinal crypts (Extended Data Fig. 3g). EdU pulse-chase labelling revealed that cycling cells, initially localized in the crypt base, progressively migrated towards the apical surface over 4 days, similar to homeostatic turnover in vivo11 (Extended Data Fig. 3h and Supplementary Video 1). These data confirm that imposing in vivo-inspired geometries on human intestinal organoids drives reproducible cell-type regionalization and migration akin to the intestinal crypt–villus axis9.

Multiplexed scRNA-seq demonstrated region-specific stem, absorptive and secretory lineages across seven donors at day 10 (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Cell-type composition was similar to primary tissue counterparts and proportions were consistent across donors, highlighting the fidelity and robustness of the system (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4c). Gene Ontology analysis of enterocyte and colonocyte marker genes revealed enrichment of distinct physiological programs concordant with the primary intestinal regions12,13 (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Proximal small intestinal enterocytes indicated higher expression of genes involving lipid, xenobiotic and iron metabolism (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). Pseudotemporal ordering of the duodenal stem-to-enterocyte trajectory confirmed enterocyte maturation levels, approaching the AQP10+ expression observed at the villus tip in vivo14 (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Distal small intestinal enterocytes expressed bile acid and vitamin B12 transport genes, whereas colonocytes were enriched in cell–cell interactions and ion transport13,15 (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). We confirmed differential protein expression of the transporters SLC5A1, SLC10A2 and SLC26A2 between the regions (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4f). Among secretory lineages, enteroendocrine cells and goblet cells were differentially abundant, with substantial heterogeneity in enteroendocrine cells (CHGA+) including EC (TPH1+), MX (GHRL+ and MLN+), D (SST+), K (GIP+), I (CCK+) and L (GCG+ and PYY+) subpopulations that match tissue distribution16 (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 4g–j).

Collectively, these data show that the engineered epithelium retains region-specific cell composition, spatial organization and gene expression, providing inroads to explore nutrient, xenobiotic and host–microbe processes in a human context.

It has been revealed that the mucus, a layered network of mucins, cellular material, antimicrobials and structural factors, provides an interactive barrier between the microbiome and intestinal epithelium. Characterizing the properties and functional role of the mucus at the host–microbe interface remains largely under-explored in vitro. To facilitate rapid accumulation of mucus, we reduced the apical volume over the course of approximately 4 days, which resulted in a fibrous mucus network covering the epithelium (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). Shed cells were present throughout the mucus layer, where they contribute to viscosity17 and can exert an antimicrobial role18 (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Longitudinal sections revealed an irregular mucus profile, with higher colonic thickness and crypt plumes similar to observations in primary tissue19 (Fig. 2c–e and Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). AlcianBlue–Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) co-staining showed regional differences in secretion and glycosylation, with higher ratios of acidic, negatively charged groups towards colon (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5h,i). These patterns were comparable with the primary tissue and may be influenced by relative levels of fucose, sialic acid and sulfate groups20. Proteomic analysis of the colonic luminal content identified the core mucus layer proteins21 (MUC2, FCGBP, TFF3, AGR2, CLCA1, ZG16 and MUC5B) as major constituents, alongside additional mucins, antimicrobials and lectin-binding proteins (Fig. 2g, Extended Data Fig. 5j and Supplementary Table 5). Using the scRNA-seq data, we identified seven non-proliferative (MKI67−) goblet cell clusters (C0–C6) representing regional diversity and differentiation state (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 5k and Supplementary Table 3). Colonic goblet cells (C1) were enriched in intracellular vesicle transport, protein glycosylation and aerobic respiration, suggesting a higher secretion machinery consistent with thickness measurements (Extended Data Fig. 5l and Supplementary Table 4).

Next, we benchmarked the expression of membrane-bound mucins, key glycocalyx components that fortify the epithelium but remain difficult to recapitulate in vitro22. We observed a strong cell-type and region-specific gene expression comparable with the reference tissue (Fig. 2i). MUC6 and MUC5AC, which encode stomach mucins that are often expressed under pathological and metaplastic conditions23,24, were nearly absent. MUC12 and MUC17 staining in the engineered epithelium and tissue counterparts confirmed the specificity and maturation of the glycocalyx, revealing in vivo-like levels by day 12 of culture (Fig. 2j,k and Extended Data Fig. 5m). Finally, we functionally assessed the mucus upon colonization with the commensals Enterococcus faecium or Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, which proliferated without compromising epithelial integrity (Fig. 2l and Extended Data Fig. 5n). Together, these results indicate that the platform can accumulate a complex mucus layer with in vivo-like and region-specific properties, opening new avenues for the study of human mucus and host–microbe interactions.

Unlike commensal microbiota, the foodborne pathogen S.Tm exploits motility and adhesion mechanisms to penetrate the mucus25, triggering an invasion-dependent inflammatory response that facilitates pathogen colonization26. Although extensive research has characterized the fundamental mechanisms underlying S.Tm infection, the exact epithelial responses and the resulting epithelial–immune signalling remain unresolved at the human level and at single-cell resolution.

In a recent development, motivated by the higher mucus level and its potential role against pathogenic bacteria, we infected colonic epithelium with S.Tm 14028 in conditions with varying densities of mucus. At 18 h post-start of the infection (hpi), S.Tm triggered strong damage in conditions with less mucus (Mucuslo), whereas the epithelium remained largely unaffected in the presence of dense mucus (Mucushi; Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Furthermore, the denser mucus led to a decrease in microbial burden, cell invasion and cytokine release, while preserving barrier integrity (Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). These protective effects were coupled with cell shedding, which predominantly localized at crypt openings, presumably impeding bacterial colonization (Extended Data Fig. 6h).
